passages.t: Isaac is born, and Sarah laughs
passages.happening:
“Now the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised” (verse 1). Sarah becomes pregnant and has a son “at the very time God had promised” (verse 2).

Abraham names him Isaac (verse 3). He circumcises him on the eighth day, as God commanded (verse 4). Abraham is a hundred years old (verse 5).

Sarah says, “God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me” (verse 6). “Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers had waited with Abraham a long time. He was seventy-five when God first promised him a family (12:4). Now he is a hundred. Twenty-five years of waiting end in two plain verses. The text says it twice, as if it can hardly believe it: as he had said, as he had promised.

‘Attended to’ translates a Hebrew word that means to visit or to turn your attention to someone and act. Joseph uses the same word at the end of Genesis, when he says God will surely come to his people and bring them out of Egypt (50:24).

Isaac's name means ‘he laughs’. Laughter has run through his whole story. Abraham laughed when God promised him a son (17:17). Sarah laughed behind the tent door because she had given up hope (18:12). Now she laughs again, and this time it is joy. And she says the whole world will laugh with her. A joke nobody believed has turned into good news.

Circumcision on the eighth day was the sign of the covenant God gave in chapter 17 (17:12). Isaac is the first child in Genesis to receive it on the very day the covenant set.
passages.later:
The pattern of a long-barren woman who bears a son by God's gift runs through the Bible: Rachel, Samson's mother, Hannah, and Elizabeth. When the angel tells Mary that her old relative Elizabeth is expecting a child, he says, “For no word from God will ever fail” (Luke 1:37).

The psalm of returning exiles sounds like Sarah: “Then our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:2).

Paul tells believers, “Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise” (Galatians 4:28). He means people who belong to God because God promised and did it, not because they made it happen.
passages.hard: A word of care. Sarah's story ends in joy, with a son in her old age. But that does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: God kept a promise that took twenty-five years. Ask what promise of God you have stopped expecting. Then notice that Sarah's laughter changed from the laugh of someone who had given up to the laugh of someone who had been given a gift.

passages.t: ‘Expel the slave woman and her son’
passages.happening:
The child grows and is weaned, and Abraham holds a great feast (verse 8).

“But Sarah saw that the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son” (verse 9). She says to Abraham, “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with my son Isaac!” (verse 10).

“Now this matter distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son Ishmael” (verse 11). But God tells him not to be distressed. “Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (verse 12). “But I will also make a nation of the slave woman’s son, because he is your offspring” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Weaning is when a child stops nursing at the mother's breast. In the ancient world it often came at two or three years old. An old Jewish book, 2 Maccabees, has a mother speak of nursing her son for three years. So many babies died young that reaching this age was worth a feast.

Ishmael is about sixteen by now. He was thirteen when he was circumcised (17:25), a year before Isaac was born.

What was Ishmael doing? The Hebrew word is from the same root as Isaac's name: he was ‘laughing’. Bibles translate it ‘mocking’ or ‘playing’. Some readers think he was making fun of the little boy. Others think he was simply playing with him, and that Sarah saw in it a threat: the older son acting as Isaac's equal. The text does not say which.

Listen to how Sarah speaks. She does not say ‘Hagar’ or ‘Ishmael’. She says ‘the slave woman’ and ‘her son’. But the narrator says this troubled Abraham ‘because it concerned his son Ishmael’ (verse 11), and God calls the boy Abraham's offspring (verse 13).

There is a legal side to this. The Laws of Hammurabi, a Babylonian law code (laws 170 and 171), say that if a father had owned a slave woman's sons as his own, they shared the inheritance; if he had not, after his death the woman and her children were to go free. The parallel is not exact. But Sarah's words are about the inheritance, and her demand meant that Ishmael would not share it.
passages.later:
Paul uses this scene in Galatians 4. He quotes Sarah's words, “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son” (Galatians 4:30). He says plainly that he is using the story as a picture, and the note on Genesis 16:13-16 explains how. His picture is about belonging to God by promise, not by human effort. It is not a verdict on Hagar or Ishmael as people, nor on any people today.

Paul also quotes God's words in verse 12: “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (Romans 9:7). He means that God's family is made by God's promise. Hebrews quotes the same words just before the story of Abraham's test (Hebrews 11:18).
passages.hard:
Does God approve of Sarah's demand? The scene is painful, and Genesis does not soften it. Sarah's words are harsh. Abraham is deeply troubled, because Ishmael is his son.

God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah, but the reason he gives is not that Sarah is right in how she speaks. The reason is that the promise will be carried through Isaac. And in the same breath God makes a promise to Ishmael: he too will be a nation, ‘because he is your offspring’. God agrees that the two lines must part. He does not agree that Ishmael is nobody. And in the next verses he himself sees to it that the boy lives.

Some readers also point out that, if the old laws stood behind this, a slave woman's son sent away and not sold left as a free person. That may be so. It does not make the sending easy.
passages.asks: Sarah could not bring herself to say Hagar's name or Ishmael's. Ask whether there is someone you can speak of only by a label. Then notice that God calls Ishmael Abraham's offspring, and promises him a future.

passages.happening:
“Early in the morning, Abraham got up, took bread and a skin of water, put them on Hagar’s shoulders, and sent her away with the boy” (verse 14). She wanders in the wilderness of Beersheba.

When the water is gone, she leaves the boy under a bush and sits down about a bowshot away. “I cannot bear to watch the boy die!” she says, and she weeps (verses 15-16).

“Then God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven” (verse 17). “What is wrong, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies” (verse 17). She is to lift him up, “for I will make him into a great nation” (verse 18).

“Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water” (verse 19). She fills the skin and gives the boy a drink. “And God was with the boy” (verse 20). He grows up in the wilderness, becomes an archer, and lives in the wilderness of Paran. His mother finds him a wife from Egypt (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
A skin of water is a bag made of animal hide. In the desert it would not last long. Abraham gives what a man can carry on his back, and sends them out. This is hard to read, and it should be.

A bowshot is the distance an arrow flies. Hagar cannot leave the boy, and she cannot bear to watch him die. So she sits where she can hear him but not see his face.

Is Ishmael a little child here? He is about sixteen, yet he seems to be laid under a bush. The Hebrew of verse 14 can be read as putting only the bread and water on Hagar's shoulder, and ‘boy’ covers a wide range of ages. A teenager dying of thirst could well be laid in the shade by his mother.

Notice whose voice God hears. Hagar weeps, but the text says God heard the voice of the boy. And he speaks through his name. Ishmael means ‘God hears’ (16:11). God does exactly what the boy's name says.

This scene echoes Genesis 16. Hagar is in the wilderness again. There is water, an angel's call, a promise of a great nation, and God's care for the one who cries. The first time, Hagar named God ‘the God who sees me’. This time God opens her eyes so that she can see.

Paran is the wilderness south of Canaan, in the north-east of Sinai. Ishmael grows up free, as the angel promised (16:12).
passages.later:
The God who hears the outcast is the God of the psalms: “This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him” (Psalm 34:6).

God keeps his word to Ishmael. Genesis lists his twelve sons as “twelve princes of their tribes” (Genesis 25:16). And when Abraham dies, “His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him” (Genesis 25:9).

The next chapter mirrors this one. Another father rises early in the morning (Genesis 22:3). Another son comes to the edge of death. Another angel calls from heaven (Genesis 22:11). Both of Abraham's sons are saved by God.
passages.hard:
This passage should not be softened. A father sends his son and the son's mother into the desert with bread and one skin of water. The mother sits down to wait for her child to die. Whatever God's purpose in parting the two lines, the cost fell on Hagar and Ishmael.

And God does not leave them. He hears, he speaks, he opens Hagar's eyes, and he is with the boy as he grows. The family sent them away. God went with them.

Muslims honor this story. In Muslim tradition Abraham brings Hagar (Hajar) and Ishmael (Ismail) to the valley where Mecca now stands. A well-known account in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari tells that Hagar asked Abraham whether God had commanded this, and when he said yes, she trusted that God would not abandon them. God then gives them water from the spring of Zamzam. The note on Genesis 16:13-16 says more. Christians and Muslims tell the story differently, but both can say what Genesis says: God heard the boy.

A word for anyone who has been sent away by a parent, or a parent who has had to let a child go. Being sent away is not the end of being seen. God heard Ishmael under that bush. If you are carrying this, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you have nowhere safe to stay, the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God heard the voice of the boy whose name means ‘God hears’. Ask who in your world has been sent away: a child, a parent, a stranger, a person someone else decided did not belong. Then ask what it would mean to hear them, as God did.

passages.t: A well, an oath and a tree at Beersheba
passages.happening:
Abimelech comes with Phicol, the commander of his army. “God is with you in all that you do,” he tells Abraham (verse 22). He asks Abraham to swear not to deal falsely with him or his children (verse 23). Abraham says, “I swear it” (verse 24).

But Abraham complains that Abimelech's servants have seized one of his wells. Abimelech says he did not know (verses 25-26). The two men make a covenant, and Abraham gives Abimelech sheep and cattle (verse 27).

Abraham sets apart seven ewe lambs. They are “my witness that I dug this well” (verse 30). “So that place was called Beersheba, because it was there that the two of them swore an oath” (verse 31).

Abimelech goes home. “And Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God” (verse 33). He lives in that land for a long time (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Beersheba is in the northern Negev, the dry south. For herders, a well meant life. Whoever controlled the well controlled who could stay. A quarrel over a well was a quarrel over survival.

A covenant here is a treaty between two people, sealed by an oath. An oath called God as witness. The seven lambs were a sign everyone could see: by taking them, Abimelech agreed that Abraham had dug this well.

The name holds a play on words. In Hebrew the word for ‘seven’ and the word for ‘swear an oath’ sound alike. So Beersheba can mean ‘well of seven’ or ‘well of the oath’.

A tamarisk is a hardy desert tree that can live a long time. Planting a tree is what someone does who means to stay.

‘The Eternal God’ translates El Olam, ‘the God of forever’. Abraham calls on the God whose life outlasts every generation, the God who can keep a promise longer than any one man lives.

‘The land of the Philistines’ is a puzzle. The Philistines known from archaeology settled on the southern coast in the 1100s BC, long after the time usually given for Abraham. Some think the writer used a later, familiar name for the region. Some think earlier groups from the Aegean Sea were already there. Some think the stories took their final shape in a later time. These notes do not settle it.
passages.later:
Isaac later comes to Beersheba, and God says to him, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you” (Genesis 26:24). Isaac builds an altar and his servants dig a well there (Genesis 26:25).

Beersheba became Israel's southern edge. The Bible speaks of the whole land as “from Dan to Beersheba” (Judges 20:1).

Isaiah names the same God: “The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary” (Isaiah 40:28).
passages.asks: Abraham settled a quarrel over water by telling the truth, making a fair agreement, and calling on God as witness. Ask whether there is a dispute in your life that could be settled that way. Then notice that Abraham, after all his failures, ends the chapter calling on the God who lasts forever.
